anti_overlap: Does not evaluate the lint suite's own check implementations (regex evasion, vacuous checks) as a static-analysis artifact — that is fd-staticanalysis-tokenlint-evasion.
Does not evaluate the getComputedStyle/MapLibre token-resolution seam or theme-change propagation — that is fd-cssvar-mapseam-runtime-integrity.
Focuses on state/contract reachability and fidelity between declared and actually-rendered UI behavior, not on token values, CSS parsing, or color math.
decision_lens: For each of the seven interaction states, each declared parts entry, and each mayNest/mustNotNest rule across the four §14 components, trace a concrete path — a real prop combination reachable from /plan (excluding the ?sw-state= QA override) or from another realistic composition — that reaches it; anywhere no such path exists, or where the override is the ONLY path, name it.
focus: The §14 component-contract layer (shadewright-contract.ts + components/shadewright/*) and the derived seven-interaction-state machine (plan-state.ts) as wired into the /plan showcase (plan/page.tsx) — whether every declared state, part, and composition rule is actually reachable by a real user, whether the CONTRACT objects the components export describe what genuinely renders, and whether the showcase's own QA machinery (the ?sw-state= override) can mask gaps rather than reveal them.
name: fd-uistatemachine-contract-fidelity
persona: Apply the perspective of a UI state-machine and component-contract reviewer who has shipped 'every component declares its states' discipline (XState-adjacent modeling, Storybook state matrices, exhaustiveness-checked union types) in production and treats a components/shadewright/index.ts-style boundary claim ('a primitive lives here if a second GSV app would want it unchanged') and a CONTRACT export as promises to be tested against the actual render tree, not the type system. This reviewer's default question for any declared-but-unverified property is: what real sequence of user actions reaches this — and if none does, is it actually part of the contract, or aspirational documentation wearing a contract's clothes?
review_areas: derivePlanState's precedence order (plan-state.ts lines 51-65: offline > denied > error > loading > stale > empty > idle) is unit-tested for reachability in isolation against a synthetic REACHES table (plan-state.test.ts), but trace it against /plan/page.tsx's actual wiring: locationPermission only ever becomes "denied" via useMyLocation's geolocation error callback (page.tsx ~185-190) — there is no independent, persisted, or on-mount permission check, so `denied` is reachable in the real app only through one specific button tap, with timing and interaction against `failed`/`loading` the isolated unit test's direct-assignment REACHES table never has to route through.

`stale` depends on `conditionAgeMs > freshnessMaxMs` (60s default), recomputed only because a `setInterval(..., 10_000)` ticks a dummy `setClock` counter to force a re-render (page.tsx ~135-153) — verify this 10-second poll is coarse enough that `stale` can visibly miss its transition for up to 10 seconds after crossing the freshness boundary, and confirm no other event (tab refocus, visibility change, route refetch) forces an earlier recheck, despite R10.1/R11.4 framing staleness as something the chrome actively watches for.

The `?sw-state=` URL override (page.tsx ~101-116, applied at line 156 as `override ?? derivePlanState(...)`) is the only practical way to reach `offline`/`stale`/arguably `denied` for manual QA — but it only replaces the derived `state` value; every other piece of page state (`route`, `weather`, `failure`) stays whatever it already was, typically null/empty on a fresh load. Visiting `/plan?sw-state=stale` never actually renders stale's own documented meaning ('we HAVE a route, but the conditions... aged,' plan-state.ts ~40-41) — only stale chrome over an empty sheet — so QA exercised through the override can be indistinguishable from genuine coverage of a state that, in reality, has never been rendered as designed.

ComfortVerdict's `mustNotNest: ["ComfortVerdict", "Sheet", "StatStrip"]` and Sheet's `mayNest: ["StatStrip", "ComfortVerdict", "Reticle"]` describe a composition graph by component name only, with nothing (lint or otherwise) verifying the four components' declarations are even mutually consistent with each other, or that plan/page.tsx's actual composition (Sheet's body rendering ComfortVerdict and StatStrip together, page.tsx ~412-437) is checked against those declarations by any mechanism at all — the CONTRACT objects may be purely descriptive metadata nobody cross-references at runtime or in CI.

Five of the seven interaction states (loading/stale/error/offline/denied) render, at the DOM level, as byte-for-byte the same `<StateNotice>` markup across ComfortVerdict/Reticle/StatStrip (only Sheet additionally keeps header/footer/children visible per its own docstring, lines 116-124) — and StateNotice itself is listed in CONTRACT_EXEMPT (shadewright-lint.ts ~657-661) specifically because its parts 'belong to the contracts of the components that declare it,' while sw-states's `p.startsWith("notice")` carve-out (shadewright-lint.ts ~774-777) exempts those parts from declared/rendered matching entirely. Nothing anywhere actually cross-checks StateNotice's contribution against any individual component's contract — verify whether 'all seven states designed' is testing per-component design work or just testing that each file remembered to import StateNotice.

INTERACTION_STATES and the ComponentContract shape are duplicated between shadewright-contract.ts (the real, imported type) and shadewright-lint.ts (a second, hand-copied literal array, per its own comment at lines 639-640: 'duplicated here so the linter has no runtime dependency on app code it is meant to police') — confirm whether anything would catch the two enums drifting apart if a future state were added to one but not the other; today they match by coincidence of careful authorship, not by any check.

severity_examples.condition: page.tsx's `?sw-state=` override (~101-116, wired at line 156) replaces only the top-level derived `state`; `route`/`weather`/`failure` remain in their pre-override shape, typically empty on a fresh load. A QA pass at `/plan?sw-state=stale` never renders stale's documented condition — 'we HAVE a route, but the conditions under it have aged past the reference clock' (plan-state.ts ~40-41) — only stale chrome floating over an empty sheet, which is a materially different render from the one the state exists to represent, and is indistinguishable from real coverage using the tooling the page itself provides.
severity_examples.scenario: The QA override can make a state look covered without ever rendering what the state means

severity_examples.condition: derivePlanState's `stale` gate (`conditionAgeMs > freshnessMaxMs`) is only re-evaluated when page.tsx's `setInterval(..., 10_000)` fires (line 147); there is no visibility-change or focus listener forcing an earlier recheck, so a route that crosses the 60-second freshness boundary while the tab is backgrounded — or simply between ticks — continues rendering as `idle` for up to 10 more seconds after it is, by the canon's own rule (R10.1, R11.4: 'stale is visible, not silent'), already stale.
severity_examples.scenario: Stale transition lags its own reference clock by up to 10 seconds with no compensating trigger

severity_examples.condition: Five of seven states render identical StateNotice markup across ComfortVerdict/Reticle/StatStrip, with the real design work centralized in a file (StateNotice.tsx) that sw-states explicitly declines to hold to its own contract (CONTRACT_EXEMPT, shadewright-lint.ts ~657-661) and whose parts are carved out of the declared/rendered check entirely (`p.startsWith("notice")`, ~774-777) — so a component's green sw-states result may be certifying only that it imported the shared primitive, not that it designed six of its own seven states.
severity_examples.scenario: Per-component 'all seven states designed' collapses to 'imports StateNotice'

success_hints: For each of the seven states in each of the four components, find (or fail to find) a real prop/composition path from /plan/page.tsx, excluding the ?sw-state= override, that reaches it — report every state/component pair whose only reachability is the override.

Load /plan?sw-state=stale (and each other override value) in a real or simulated session and diff what actually renders against derivePlanState's own documented meaning for that state (the precedence-order comments in plan-state.ts lines 32-50) — flag any mismatch between 'the state label is showing' and 'the situation the state represents is showing.'

Check whether any mechanism cross-validates a pair of components' mayNest/mustNotNest declarations for mutual consistency, or whether plan/page.tsx's actual composition (Sheet containing both ComfortVerdict and StatStrip) is checked against those declarations anywhere in lint or tests.

Compare the six non-idle branches across ComfortVerdict/Reticle/Sheet/StatStrip for how much each actually differs beyond 'wraps StateNotice,' and ask whether sw-states is verifying seven designed states or seven imported ones.
Verify INTERACTION_STATES stays byte-identical between shadewright-contract.ts and shadewright-lint.ts, and check whether anything would fail today if a state were added to one but not the other.
task_context: find defects, gaps and false confidence in the Shadewright IMPLEMENTATION (not the canon, already reviewed). Focus: checks that pass vacuously or are trivially evaded; canon rules that NO check enforces; states declared but unreachable; the getComputedStyle token-resolution seam and its failure modes; and anywhere the enforcement suite reports green while the rendered page is wrong — three classes already silently compiled to nothing this session (a bad Tailwind border utility, an undefined `wide:` variant, and an undeclared --color-bg). Weight lib/shadewright-contract.ts, lib/plan-state.ts, components/shadewright/*, and app/plan/page.tsx most heavily; treat shadewright-lint.ts's sw-states check as the enforcement mechanism whose blind spots this agent exists to find from the product/state-machine side.
